candidate.answerReason: There is exactly one circular arrangement missing sum 6 and exactly one missing sum 7, up to rotation and reflection. These cases are distinct and exhaust the bad arrangements.

methods.label: Complementary sums and forced neighbors
methods.explanation:
The total of the five numbers is \(15\). The complement of any proper consecutive block is another consecutive block, so a sum \(n\) is available exactly when \(15-n\) is available. Single numbers supply sums \(1\) through \(5\), their complements supply \(10\) through \(14\), and the whole circle supplies \(15\). Thus an arrangement is good exactly when sums \(6\) and \(7\) are both available; their complements then supply \(9\) and \(8\).

The only subsets summing to \(6\) are \(\{1,5\}\), \(\{2,4\}\), and \(\{1,2,3\}\). On a five-number circle, three numbers form a consecutive block exactly when the other two numbers are adjacent. Consequently, sum \(6\) is available exactly when at least one of the pairs \(1,5\), \(2,4\), or \(4,5\) is adjacent.

Similarly, the only subsets summing to \(7\) are \(\{2,5\}\), \(\{3,4\}\), and \(\{1,2,4\}\). Thus sum \(7\) is available exactly when at least one of the pairs \(2,5\), \(3,4\), or \(3,5\) is adjacent.

Suppose sum \(6\) is missing. Then \(4\) cannot neighbor \(2\) or \(5\), so its neighbors must be \(1\) and \(3\). Also, \(5\) cannot neighbor \(1\) or \(4\), so its neighbors must be \(2\) and \(3\). These requirements force the path \(1,4,3,5,2\), whose endpoints must be joined. Up to rotation and reflection, this gives the single circle
\[
(1,2,5,3,4).
\]
It avoids all three pairs that would supply sum \(6\), and it has sum \(7=2+5\).

Suppose instead that sum \(7\) is missing. Then \(3\) must neighbor \(1\) and \(2\), while \(5\) must neighbor \(1\) and \(4\). Closing the resulting path gives the single circle
\[
(1,3,2,4,5).
\]
It avoids all three pairs that would supply sum \(7\), and it has sum \(6=1+5\).

Every bad arrangement belongs to one of these two cases. Each case gives exactly one arrangement up to the stated symmetries, and the cases do not overlap because each arrangement has the sum missing from the other. Therefore there are \(\boxed{2}\) bad arrangements, choice B.
